# Processing with SNAP

`BurstProcessor` turns downloaded bursts into geocoded GeoTIFFs. It runs
SNAP once for every burst, or once for every pair of bursts, and skips products
that already exist.

## How a processing call works

Every `create_*` method takes the bursts, the UTM zone of the output, and
optionally a settings object. From the settings, s1bursts builds the SNAP
processing graph, the chain of SNAP steps that turns a burst into a product.
The settings describe how to process and suit every burst alike. The UTM zone
depends on where the bursts are, so it is passed separately as `crs`, the
coordinate reference system (CRS):

```{.python}
from s1bursts import BurstProcessor, RTCConfig

processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, crs="auto", config=RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20))
```

Products are always projected in a WGS 84 / UTM zone. `crs="auto"` takes each
burst's own zone, its `utm_zone`, which suits bursts used on their own, such as
a time series: the zone depends only on the footprint, so every date of a burst
lands in the same one. To fix the zone instead, pass it as a string, an EPSG
code or a `pyproj.CRS`, such as `crs="EPSG:32632"` for zone 32 North.

If you plan to [composite](compositing.qmd), choose the zone before processing:
a composite accepts only products in the UTM zone and pixel size of its grid
square, so process them with `crs=square.crs`. Without `config`, the defaults
apply, and they suit most uses.

Each product has its own method and settings object:

| Method | Input | Settings | Product |
|---|---|---|---|
| `create_backscatter()` | Bursts | `RTCConfig` or `GTCConfig` | Backscatter of each acquisition |
| `create_coherences()` | Pairs | `CoherenceConfig` | Coherence between two acquisitions |

The settings objects share most fields. The one you are most likely to change
is the pixel size, `grid_spacing`, which is 10 m by default. A smaller pixel
size does not add detail beyond what the radar resolves. The
[API reference](../reference/snap_graph.RTCConfig.qmd) lists every setting and
its default.

[SNAP processing](snap-processing.qmd) explains the steps each graph runs and
how to inspect the graph your settings produce.

## Backscatter

Backscatter describes how strongly the ground reflects the radar signal on one
date. In mountains, it also depends on the angle of each slope to the
satellite: slopes facing the satellite look bright, and slopes facing away look
dark. By default, s1bursts removes this effect with radiometric terrain
correction (RTC), following the terrain-flattening method of
Small (2011)[^small]. RTC divides each
pixel by the area of ground that contributed to it, so the remaining
differences in brightness come from the surface itself. The result is called
gamma-0.

Use RTC unless you have a reason not to. Only RTC products can be composited
with [resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd). The settings object
selects the product: `RTCConfig`, the default, gives RTC, and `GTCConfig` gives
geometrically terrain-corrected (GTC) backscatter, called beta-0,
which places pixels correctly on the map but keeps the slope brightness:

```{.python}
from s1bursts import GTCConfig

gtc = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, crs="auto", config=GTCConfig())
```

## Coherence

Coherence measures how similar two acquisitions of the same footprint are, from
0 to 1. It drops wherever the surface changed between the two dates, for
example through snowfall, melt, vegetation growth or movement, such as the
flow of a glacier. The pairs come from
[`find_pairs()`](finding-and-downloading.qmd#pair-acquisitions):

```{.python}
pairs = bursts.find_pairs(baseline=12)
coherence = processor.create_coherences(pairs, crs="auto")
```

The product contains the coherence magnitude: the absolute value of the complex
correlation between the two acquisitions, estimated over a small window of
neighboring pixels set by `CoherenceConfig(window=...)`. A larger window gives
smoother values at a coarser resolution. The phase of the correlation is not
kept, and s1bursts makes no interferograms. ASF's
[HyP3 burst InSAR](https://hyp3-docs.asf.alaska.edu/guides/burst_insar_product_guide)
products cover the same bursts with wrapped and unwrapped phase.

## Run several jobs at once

`SNAPConfig` sets how many SNAP processes run in parallel and how much memory
they share. Pass it to the processor to override the
[environment variables](environment-variables.qmd#snap):

```{.python}
from s1bursts import SNAPConfig

processor = BurstProcessor(fm, config=SNAPConfig(max_workers=2, max_ram_gb=16))
```

More processes finish a batch sooner but split the memory budget between them.
If SNAP runs out of memory, use fewer processes or a larger budget.

## Reprocessing and failures

A product whose file already exists is not processed again, so a script can be
rerun after an interruption.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Changed settings raise an error

Filenames describe the burst and date, not the settings, so an existing file is
checked before it is skipped. If it was made with other settings, such as
another `grid_spacing` or DEM, the call raises a `ProductSettingsMismatchError`
naming each difference, before SNAP runs. The same error is raised for a file that does not
record every setting, such as one written by an earlier s1bursts version, and
for a file made by another SNAP version, since the versions give slightly different
results (see [SNAP versions](snap-processing.qmd#snap-versions)). A SNAP
version that could not be determined is not compared. Write each experiment to
its own `FileManager` directory, or pass `overwrite=True` to replace the old
products.
:::

A failed burst does not stop the batch by default. Each call returns an
`OperationSummary`. Check it before using the results, since a time series
with silent gaps can mislead. `raise_on_failure()` raises an error listing
every failed burst, and otherwise returns the summary, so its products are one
step away:

```{.python}
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, crs="auto").raise_on_failure().products
```

Pass `continue_on_error=False` to `BurstProcessor` to stop at the first failure
instead.

[^small]: Small, D. (2011). Flattening gamma: Radiometric terrain correction
    for SAR imagery. *IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing*,
    49(8), 3081–3093. <https://doi.org/10.1109/TGRS.2011.2120616>
